(CNN) -- In the pre-dawn darkness Saturday, long after her parents and brother were asleep, Atefeh Yazdi lay in bed cradling the house phone and her cell phone in her hands. Atefeh Yazdi visits with her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi, during his trip to America last year. The only light was from a television tuned to the latest news from Iran, and her laptop displaying her Facebook page in hope of any updates on what was happening halfway around the world. "I kind of felt I was more there when I couldn't see the rest of the room, just the TV and the Facebook," the 28-year-old Iranian-American told CNN by telephone from her home in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania. Repeated calls to relatives in Tehran only got the "annoying" Farsi-language error message. She recounted the thoughts running through her brain all night: "Are they going to really shoot people? What's going to happen? Is this going to turn into massive killing and violence?" In Houston, Texas, Reza Soltani said the anxiety of waiting and wondering was like endless pacing at a hospital during a loved one's operation. "It feels like the operation started last week and it hasn't ended," Soltani, 28, told CNN by telephone. "I'm worried. I'm hoping it will be good but I'm worried it will get very ugly." The jumble of emotions -- fear, hope, anxiety, frustration -- were reality for millions of Iranian-Americans trying to find out if Iranian authorities would crush protests over last week's election. President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the overwhelming victor in voting that opposition groups called rigged. No independent monitors were permitted for the election. A threatening statement Friday by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei increased fears of bloodshed. Iranian authorities have cut off traditional communications such as cell phone connections, and also banned foreign news outlets from covering the protests. Thousands of protesters took to the streets Saturday, even though the demonstrations were banned and police confronted them with clubs, tear gas and water cannons. The uncertainty and unrest strikes close to home for Yazdi, whose grandfather -- a longtime politician in Iran -- was arrested from his hospital bed this week. He's been returned to the hospital, she said, but she doesn't know if he'll be arrested again or what will happen to other relatives. "It's very exhausting," Yazdi said. "I have this feeling I want to be there. I want to book the next flight. I want to be with the people. I don't care about the risks involved." Her parents, who left Iran in the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution, say such talk is foolish, she said. They are as worried as she is, but fear returning now would bring too much risk. "There's a generation gap, a culture gap," she explained. It runs deep, defining her life as an American-born citizen of both Iran and the United States, who refers to Iranians as "my people." "Being born and raised in America, where I was able to voice my opinion, do what I want, say what I wanted, I'm culturally confused," Yazdi said. "I'm not completely American the right way, and I'm not completely Iranian the right way." Soltani also mentioned the generation gap among Iranian-Americans, but he described it as more political. His parents' generation lost everything in the revolution, and will only consider returning when the revolutionary regime has been toppled, he said. Older Iranian-Americans in the United States "actually boycotted the election, saying if you vote you're just legitimizing the government," Soltani said. "We sacrificed everything for you guys, and now you're going to the other team," is how Soltani characterized their attitude. "They think the system needs to go completely," he said. "All they care is for the system to collapse. They think if the system collapses, they're going to be able to go back." No matter what happens, Soltani and Yazdi said, Iran is changed forever by this week's events. "I believe that anything that comes out of it will be positive," Soltani said. "Even if they fail now, the people know if they get in the streets in millions, they're not going to be able to stop them."

outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- In the pre-dawn darkness Saturday, long after her parents and brother had drifted off to sleep, Atefeh Yazdi lay awake in bed, cradling both her house phone and cell phone. The only illumination came from a television tuned to the latest news from Iran and her laptop, its screen aglow with her Facebook page, as she searched for any updates on the unfolding events halfway around the world.

"I kind of felt I was more there when I couldn't see the rest of the room, just the TV and the Facebook," the 28-year-old Iranian-American told CNN by telephone from her home in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania. Her repeated calls to relatives in Tehran yielded only the "annoying" Farsi-language error message. She described the thoughts that consumed her throughout the night: "Are they going to really shoot people? What's going to happen? Is this going to turn into massive killing and violence?"

In Houston, Texas, Reza Soltani likened the anguish of waiting and wondering to the endless pacing of a hospital corridor during a loved one's surgery. "It feels like the operation started last week and it hasn't ended," the 28-year-old told CNN by telephone. "I'm worried. I'm hoping it will be good, but I'm worried it will get very ugly."

This tangle of emotions—fear, hope, anxiety, frustration—has become the daily reality for millions of Iranian-Americans as they wait to learn whether Iranian authorities will crush the protests erupting over last week's election. President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the overwhelming victor in a vote that opposition groups have decried as rigged; no independent monitors were permitted to observe the proceedings. A menacing statement issued Friday by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has only deepened fears of impending bloodshed. Iranian authorities have severed conventional lines of communication, including cell phone networks, and barred foreign news outlets from covering the unrest.

Despite an official ban on demonstrations, thousands of protesters flooded the streets Saturday, confronting police armed with clubs, tear gas, and water cannons.

For Yazdi, this uncertainty strikes especially close to home: her grandfather, a longtime Iranian politician, was arrested this past week directly from his hospital bed. Though he has since been returned to the hospital, she remains uncertain whether he will be arrested again, or what fate awaits other relatives. "It's very exhausting," Yazdi said. "I have this feeling I want to be there. I want to book the next flight. I want to be with the people. I don't care about the risks involved."

Her parents, who fled Iran in the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution, dismiss such talk as reckless, she said. Though they share her anxiety, they fear that returning now would expose her to unacceptable danger. "There's a generation gap, a culture gap," she explained—one that runs deep, shaping her identity as an American-born citizen of both Iran and the United States, someone who nonetheless refers to Iranians as "my people."

"Being born and raised in America, where I was able to voice my opinion, do what I want, say what I wanted, I'm culturally confused," Yazdi said. "I'm not completely American the right way, and I'm not completely Iranian the right way."

Soltani, too, spoke of a generational divide among Iranian-Americans, though he framed it in more political terms. His parents' generation, having lost everything in the revolution, will only consider returning once the current regime has been toppled, he explained. Many older Iranian-Americans, he noted, "actually boycotted the election, saying if you vote you're just legitimizing the government."

"We sacrificed everything for you guys, and now you're going to the other team"—this, Soltani said, captures their prevailing attitude. "They think the system needs to go completely," he added. "All they care about is the system collapsing. They believe that if it does, they'll finally be able to go home."

Whatever the outcome, both Soltani and Yazdi agree that Iran has been irrevocably transformed by this week's events. "I believe that anything that comes out of it will be positive," Soltani said. "Even if they fail now, the people know that if they take to the streets in the millions, no one will be able to stop them."

(CNN) -- Before sunrise on Saturday, well after her family had gone to bed, Atefeh Yazdi lay awake in bed, clutching both her landline receiver and mobile phone. A photo shows Atefeh Yazdi spending time with her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi, during a visit he made to the United States the previous year. The only illumination in the room came from a television broadcasting updates from Iran and her laptop screen, open to Facebook, where she hoped to find fresh information about events unfolding on the other side of the globe. "Somehow, when I couldn't see anything else in the room besides the TV and Facebook, I felt closer to what was happening there," the 28-year-old Iranian-American explained to CNN over the phone from her residence in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania. Every time she dialed relatives in Tehran, she encountered nothing but the frustrating Farsi error recording. Throughout the night, various worries consumed her thoughts: "Would they actually open fire on people? What would happen next? Could this spiral into widespread bloodshed and violence?"

Meanwhile, in Houston, Texas, 28-year-old Reza Soltani compared his experience of anxious waiting to pacing anxiously in a hospital waiting room during a family member's surgery. "It's as though the surgery began last week and still hasn't concluded," he shared with CNN during a phone interview. "I'm anxious about it. I hope things turn out well, but I'm afraid it could become extremely violent."

This mixture of dread, optimism, nervousness, and irritation was shared by countless Iranian-Americans as they waited to learn whether Iran's government would suppress protests sparked by the previous week's contested election. Officials had announced Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the clear winner, though opposition supporters claimed the results were manipulated, and no independent election observers had been allowed to monitor the process. Concerns about violence grew after Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued an ominous warning on Friday. Authorities in Iran had already shut down standard communication channels, including cell phone service, while blocking international media from reporting on the demonstrations.

Despite an official ban on protests, thousands of demonstrators filled the streets Saturday, facing off against police who used batons, tear gas, and water cannons to disperse them.

For Yazdi, the turmoil hit particularly close to home—her grandfather, a veteran Iranian politician, had been taken into custody directly from his hospital room earlier that week. Although he was later brought back to the hospital, she remained uncertain whether he would be detained again, or what might happen to other family members. "It's incredibly draining," she admitted. "Part of me just wants to be there. I want to catch the next flight and stand with the people, regardless of the danger." Her parents, who fled Iran during the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution took hold, considered such notions reckless, she said—though they shared her worry, they believed going back now would be far too dangerous.

"There's this divide between generations, a cultural disconnect," she said, describing how it shaped her identity as someone born in America to parents from Iran—someone who nonetheless calls Iranians "my people." "Growing up in America, where I could speak my mind and live as I chose, left me feeling culturally torn," Yazdi said. "I'm not fully American in the traditional sense, and I'm not fully Iranian either."

Soltani echoed this idea of a generational rift among Iranian-Americans, though he framed it in more political terms. He explained that his parents' generation had lost everything because of the revolution and wouldn't consider returning to Iran until the current regime was overthrown. Many older Iranian-Americans, he noted, had chosen to boycott the election entirely, arguing that voting would only legitimize the government. He summarized their perspective as essentially saying, "We gave up everything for your generation, and now you're siding with them." According to Soltani, "They believe the entire system must be dismantled. Their only concern is watching it collapse completely, because they think that's when they'll finally be able to return."

Regardless of the outcome, both Soltani and Yazdi agreed that Iran had been permanently transformed by that week's events. "I truly believe something positive will emerge from all this," Soltani said. "Even if the movement doesn't succeed right now, people have realized that once millions take to the streets, no one can hold them back."

# The Long Night: Iranian-Americans Watch and Wait

Atefeh Yazdi did not sleep. The 28-year-old Iranian-American spent the night in a strange, split reality—physically present in her own home, yet emotionally transported thousands of miles away to the streets of Tehran. Her eyes moved constantly between two screens: the television, tuned to breaking news coverage of the escalating crisis in Iran, and her laptop, refreshing Facebook feeds that carried real-time updates, photos, and desperate messages from people on the ground. In that liminal space between digital connection and physical distance, Yazdi found herself feeling more tethered to the unfolding events in Iran than to the quiet, unchanging room around her. The crisis had become, in a very real sense, more present to her than her own surroundings.

Throughout the night, she tried repeatedly to reach relatives in Tehran, her fingers dialing familiar numbers with mounting urgency. Each attempt ended the same way: not with a ringing phone or a beloved voice, but with a cold, mechanical error message in Farsi—a small but maddening reminder of how thoroughly communication had broken down between her and the people she loved most.

She was not alone in this experience. In Houston, Reza Soltani, also 28, found himself gripped by a similar helplessness. He described the experience in visceral terms, likening it to the agonizing wait outside an operating room while a loved one undergoes surgery—that particular blend of hope and dread, where you cling to the possibility of good news while bracing yourself for the worst. Soltani hoped desperately for a peaceful resolution, even as he feared that violence might be the more likely outcome.

Across the United States, millions of Iranian-Americans found themselves caught in this same emotional limbo. Fear, hope, and anxiety intertwined as they waited to learn whether Iranian authorities would move to violently suppress the protests that had erupted following a deeply disputed election. The vote had declared Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the winner, but the result came without any independent verification or international monitoring, fueling widespread suspicion of fraud and igniting outrage both inside Iran and among its diaspora abroad.

That outrage seemed only more justified as the Iranian government took steps that heightened fears of an imminent and violent crackdown. A stern, threatening statement from Ayatollah Khamenei signaled that authorities had little tolerance left for dissent. Compounding the sense of dread, the government moved to sever cell phone communications across the country and barred foreign media from covering the unrest directly—actions that seemed designed to control the narrative and isolate protesters from the watching world. Yet despite these efforts at suppression, and in direct defiance of an official ban on demonstrations, thousands of protesters poured into the streets, refusing to be silenced even as the risks around them grew more severe.

For Iranian-Americans like Yazdi and Soltani, watching from afar, the night stretched on with no clear resolution—only the agonizing rhythm of refreshing pages, redialing numbers, and waiting for word from a homeland that felt, in that moment, both impossibly distant and achingly close.

# Watching from Afar: Iranian-Americans Anxiously Track Unrest Back Home

In living rooms across the United States, Iranian-Americans have found themselves glued to television screens, refreshing Facebook feeds, and dialing overseas phone numbers with trembling hands, desperate for any word on the safety of loved ones caught in the chaos unfolding thousands of miles away in Iran.

Atefeh Yazdi, like countless others in her position, has barely slept since the disputed election results were announced. "Every time the phone rings, my heart stops," she said, describing the agonizing uncertainty that has become her new normal. Her relatives in Tehran have become increasingly difficult to reach as authorities have moved to restrict communication channels throughout the country.

Reza Soltani shares similar fears. He spends hours each day scrolling through social media posts, piecing together fragments of information from citizen journalists on the ground, since traditional news outlets have been barred from providing independent coverage of the unrest. "Facebook has become our lifeline," Soltani explained. "It's often more reliable than what little official news trickles out."

The situation grew more tense after Ayatollah Khamenei issued a stern warning to protesters, signaling that authorities would not tolerate continued demonstrations against the disputed election results. In the aftermath of his statement, phone lines across Iran experienced significant disruptions, making it even harder for families abroad to confirm the wellbeing of their relatives.

Foreign media have been officially banned from covering the unrest firsthand, forcing journalists to rely on secondhand accounts, smuggled footage, and social media posts to piece together the reality on the ground. This information blackout has only heightened the anxiety felt by the diaspora community, who must now depend on unverified reports and sporadic communication to understand what is truly happening.

Despite the crackdown and the looming threat of severe consequences, thousands of Iranians have continued to take to the streets in a remarkable display of defiance. Images and videos—smuggled out through whatever means possible—show massive crowds undeterred by the government's warnings, continuing to demand accountability over the contested election results.

For Iranian-Americans watching from afar, this courage is a source of both immense pride and deepening dread. Many fear that Khamenei's hardline stance could be a precursor to a violent crackdown, with security forces potentially authorized to use force against demonstrators. The specter of bloodshed hangs heavily over every phone call and news update.

"We are proud of our people for standing up, but we are terrified of what might happen next," Yazdi said, articulating the conflicting emotions felt by many in her community. As the situation continues to evolve, Iranian-Americans remain locked in a state of helpless vigilance, their attention fixed on distant streets where the fate of their families—and their homeland—hangs in the balance.

counterfactuals.output:
# Iranian-Americans Glued to Screens as Homeland Erupts in Protest

**By CNN Staff**

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — In a suburb of Los Angeles sometimes called "Tehrangeles" for its large Iranian population, Sara Hosseini has not slept more than four hours a night since the disputed June 12 presidential election in Iran plunged her homeland into chaos.

"I have three browser tabs open at all times — Twitter, Facebook, and a Persian news site," said Hosseini, 34, who left Iran with her family as a child. "I refresh them like it's a job. When the internet gets cut off there, even for an hour, my stomach drops."

Hosseini is far from alone. Across the United States, in cities with significant Iranian-American communities — Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., New York, and Houston among them — Iranian expatriates are experiencing the unrest in Iran with an intensity that mixes hope, fear, and helplessness.

The disputed re-election of President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad over challenger Mir Hossein Mousavi has triggered the largest protests in Iran since the 1979 revolution. Demonstrators have flooded the streets of Tehran and other cities, alleging widespread vote-rigging, while the government has responded with a violent crackdown, mass arrests, and severe restrictions on foreign media and internet access.

For the Iranian diaspora — estimated at more than one million people in the U.S. — the images trickling out via cell phone video and social media have made the crisis feel painfully close, even from thousands of miles away.

## "We Are Their Voice Now"

With international journalists largely barred from independent reporting inside Iran, ordinary citizens have turned to Twitter, YouTube, and Facebook to broadcast footage of protests, beatings, and arrests. Iranian-Americans say they have taken on an informal role as translators and amplifiers of that content for the outside world.

"We are their voice now," said Kamran Amir, a 45-year-old software engineer in Northern Virginia who has spent his evenings translating Farsi tweets into English and forwarding them to media contacts. "The government is trying to silence them, so we do what we can from here — we retweet, we translate, we call reporters."

Amir said he has relatives in Tehran he has been unable to reach for days. "You send a text and you don't know if it went through, if they're okay, if they've been arrested. It's agonizing."

Community organizations have also mobilized. Solidarity rallies have taken place in Los Angeles, Washington, New York, and other cities, drawing thousands of demonstrators waving green banners and photographs of those killed or detained.

"Green has become our color of hope," said Parisa Nourbakhsh, an organizer of a rally outside the United Nations in New York. "Whether or not people here have family in Iran, this is personal. This is about the country we or our parents come from wanting to be heard."

## Fear for Family, Frustration with Coverage

For many, the anxiety is not abstract. Nasrin Tehrani, a 58-year-old physician in Chicago, said her sister in Tehran was struck by a police baton while attempting to document a demonstration on her phone.

"She told me, 'Don't worry, it's not that bad,' but I could hear it in her voice — she was terrified," Tehrani said. "I feel guilty being safe here while she is in danger there."

Some in the community have also voiced frustration with what they see as inconsistent coverage in the American press, urging continued international attention even as access to information from inside Iran becomes more difficult.

"The world cannot look away just because the government has cut off the internet," said Reza Fanaei, a professor of Middle Eastern studies who has been consulting with several news organizations. "If anything, that is exactly the moment when the world needs to pay closer attention."

## A Generation Watching, and Waiting

For younger Iranian-Americans, many born in the U.S. and with no direct memory of Iran, the protests have sparked a renewed connection to a homeland they know largely through their parents' stories.

"I've asked my dad more questions about 1979 in the last week than in my whole life," said Bijan Rostami, a 22-year-old college student in Austin, Texas, whose parents fled Iran three decades ago. "He keeps saying this feels different — that people aren't afraid anymore, even with everything happening to them."

Whether that optimism proves justified remains uncertain. As night fell in Tehran on Wednesday, the government continued to restrict access to foreign media and reportedly detained additional protesters and journalists. For Iranian-Americans anxiously monitoring events from thousands of miles away, the waiting — and the worry — continues.

"All we can do is watch, and hope, and refresh the page," Hosseini said. "And pray that when we wake up, we're waking up to good news."

*CNN's coverage of developments in Iran continues as access to information from the country remains limited.*

# Voices from the Diaspora: Iranian-Americans Reflect on 2009

*The following is a human-interest piece incorporating composite first-person perspectives reflecting common sentiments expressed by Iranian-Americans during the 2009 election crisis. Names have been changed, and these accounts are illustrative rather than verified individual testimonies.*

---

When the news broke that Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had been declared the winner of Iran's 2009 presidential election by a landslide margin—hours before many polling stations had even closed counting—phones across Iranian-American communities in Los Angeles, New York, and beyond began ringing before dawn.

## "I Hadn't Cried About Iran in Years"

*Roya, 54, Los Angeles*

"My daughter called me at 4 a.m. because she'd seen it on Twitter before it hit the news channels. I remember sitting on the edge of my bed, still in the dark, just holding the phone.

I left Iran in 1983. I've built an entire life here—my kids were born here, English is stronger than my Farsi now for them. But that morning, something in me that I thought had gone quiet woke up. I hadn't cried about Iran in years, and suddenly I couldn't stop.

We started calling family in Tehran, in Isfahan. My cousin's daughter had waited in line for hours to vote for Mousavi. She told me, 'Khaleh, we did this. We voted. And they're lying to our faces.' I could hear the anger, but also this exhaustion, like she already knew how it would end."

## "Every Video Was a Message From Home"

*Kaveh, 29, Washington D.C.*

"I was glued to my laptop for weeks. YouTube, Twitter, whatever grainy cell phone footage people could smuggle out. You'd see these massive crowds—the Silence March, hundreds of thousands of people just walking without chanting, without banners, just walking in silence as a form of protest. It gave me chills.

Then came the video of Neda Agha-Soltan. I watched it once and I still see it when I close my eyes sometimes. A young woman, shot in the street, bleeding out while people around her scream and try to help. She became this symbol overnight, but she was just a person. She was 26. My age, basically.

I organized a small vigil here in D.C. We didn't have thousands of people, but we had Iranians and non-Iranians standing together holding candles, saying her name."

## "My Parents Wouldn't Answer the Phone"

*Sara, 33, San Francisco*

"The scariest part wasn't the protests themselves—it was the silence after. We'd hear about arrests, about people disappearing into Evin Prison, and then for days I couldn't reach my parents in Tehran. The government was cutting cell service, blocking sites.

When my mother finally picked up, she spoke in code. She wouldn't say 'protest'—she'd say 'the gathering.' She wouldn't say names. You could feel her choosing every word like she was walking through a minefield.

That's when it hit me how different our worlds were, even though we're the same family. I was retweeting hashtags from my apartment with fast Wi-Fi, perfectly safe. She was terrified a knock on the door meant they'd taken my brother."

## "We Became Accidental Journalists"

*Bijan, 41, Los Angeles*

"A group of us—just regular people, an engineer, a grad student, a guy who owned a rug shop—we ended up running this makeshift news network. We had contacts feeding us information from inside Iran because international journalists were being expelled or restricted.

I'd get a voice memo at 2 a.m. from someone in Shiraz, translate it, verify what I could, and get it to contacts at news desks. It felt surreal. None of us were trained for this. We were just Iranian-Americans who couldn't sit still while our people were being beaten in the streets and the world's media had limited access.

I didn't sleep for what felt like a month."

## "I Felt Guilty for Being Safe"

*Leila, 26, New York*

"There's a specific kind of guilt in watching your people get shot at while you're sipping coffee in Brooklyn. I marched in solidarity protests here, I donated to organizations helping get information out, I called my representatives. But it never felt like enough.

My grandmother, before she passed, used to tell me stories about 1979—how hope curdles, how revolutions get hijacked. Watching 2009 unfold, I kept thinking: are we watching that same story again? Young people risking everything for change, and an old guard determined to crush it before it can breathe.

I still don't know how that story ends. I'm not sure Iran does either."

---

## A Diaspora Watching, Waiting

What emerged from that summer was not just outrage but a complicated intimacy with a country many had left behind, physically, decades earlier. The Green Movement, as it came to be known, didn't topple the government. Ahmadinejad remained in office. But for many Iranian-Americans, the crackdown reshaped something quieter and more personal: a reconnection with grief, with hope, and with a homeland that remained, despite distance and years, inescapably theirs.

The unrest following President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's contested re-election has turned social media into a lifeline—and a source of torment—for families separated by the distance and, increasingly, by government efforts to choke off communication. Text messaging has been intermittently blocked inside Iran, and internet speeds have been deliberately throttled, according to several diaspora members who described trying, and failing, to reach relatives.

"My sister was supposed to call me Saturday morning," said Kamran Ashtiani, 34, an engineer in Los Angeles who asked that his sister's name be withheld out of concern for her safety. "She didn't. For many, the anguish is compounded by history. Some fled Iran after the 1979 revolution or during the brutal crackdowns of the 1980s, and the current images have reopened old wounds.

"I watched my own generation get crushed thirty years ago," said Farideh Goldin, an author and professor who left Iran as a young woman. "Now I'm watching it happen to my nieces and nephews, to young people who weren't even born when I left. I thought I had buried this fear. I hadn't. It was just waiting."

Younger Iranian-Americans, many of them born or raised in the U.S., describe a different but equally consuming form of anxiety—one shaped by round-the-clock exposure to unverified footage on Twitter and YouTube.

"I'm scrolling through videos of people getting beaten in the street, and I don't know if that's my cousin's neighborhood or not," said Sara Rostami, a 22-year-old student at UCLA. "I've never lived in Iran. I've only visited a few times. But somehow this feels like it's happening to me too. I think it's happening to all of us."

"I keep asking myself what I'm supposed to do with this feeling," said Ashtiani. "I can't march in those streets. All I can do is watch, and hope, and wait for my phone to ring."

# The Distance That Wasn't: How Diaspora Iranians Bridged an Ocean During the Green Movement

*A feature on connection, fear, and technology during Iran's 2009 election crisis*

When Neda Agha-Soltan died on a Tehran street on June 20, 2009, her final moments captured on a shaky cell phone video, Sara Mostafavi was sitting in her apartment in Los Angeles, refreshing Twitter every thirty seconds.

"I hadn't slept in four days," she recalls. "My phone was basically surgically attached to my hand. I kept thinking—what if the next video is of someone I know?"

For Iranian-Americans, the disputed re-election of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad and the protests that followed weren't distant news events. They were family emergencies playing out in real time, six thousand miles away, filtered through a patchwork of technology that became, for a few extraordinary weeks, a lifeline between two worlds.

## The Blackout

When the Iranian government began restricting internet access and cutting mobile networks in the days following the June 12 election, it did more than silence protesters—it severed generations of families from each other at the exact moment they most needed to connect.

"My mother would call and the line would just cut off mid-sentence," says Kamran Delshad, an engineer in the Bay Area whose parents still lived in Tehran's Vanak district. "You'd hear 'they're saying the Basij are on—' and then nothing. Silence. For hours you don't know if it's the phone line or if something happened to your mother."

Delshad describes downloading proxy server lists that circulated through diaspora email chains, then relaying them back to cousins in Iran via text message—a strange, backwards flow of technical support crossing the same ocean that usually carried nostalgia and grocery-list requests for saffron and pistachios.

"I became this weird IT support desk for half my extended family," he says. "I'd never even met some of these cousins in person. Suddenly I'm their lifeline to the outside world."

## Twitter as Town Square, Newsroom, and Vigil

With international journalists expelled or confined to hotel rooms, Twitter became an improvised wire service—unreliable, unverified, but immediate. The hashtag #IranElection trended globally for days. Iranian-Americans became de facto translators and fact-checkers, converting Persian-language tweets into English for a Western audience hungry for information.

Roya Hakimian, a graduate student in Chicago at the time, remembers spending entire nights monitoring accounts believed to belong to protesters in Tehran.

"You'd see a username you recognized go quiet for six hours, and your stomach would just drop," she says. "Then they'd post again—'still alive, don't worry'—and you'd feel this insane relief for someone you'd never met and never would meet."

Hakimian's own connection was more direct: her younger brother, a student at Tehran University, was texting her updates using code words the family had developed over frantic phone calls, worried about surveillance.

"We called the Ministry of Intelligence building 'the dentist.' Getting arrested was 'catching a cold.' It sounds almost silly now, but at the time it felt like the only way to communicate something true."

## The Weight of Watching

For many Iranian-Americans, the crisis exposed a particular anguish: the helplessness of diaspora life. They could organize solidarity rallies in Los Angeles, Washington, and New York—and they did, by the thousands, wearing green and chanting names that would soon become martyrs. But they could not do the one thing that mattered most: protect the people they loved.

Farah Ansari, who left Iran in 1998 and settled in Virginia, describes the specific torture of watching protest videos hoping—and dreading—that she might spot her sister's face in the crowd.

"I would slow down videos of Azadi Square, frame by frame, looking for her red scarf," Ansari says. "I never found her. I don't know if that made it better or worse."

Her sister eventually called using a friend's phone from Turkey, having crossed the border to make contact.

"She said, 'I'm fine, don't worry'—and then she started crying, and I started crying, and neither of us said anything for probably two full minutes. We just cried together on the phone, six thousand miles apart."

## A Generation's First Political Awakening

For younger Iranian-Americans—many born in the U.S. or raised there from childhood—2009 became a formative moment of political identity, often their first sustained engagement with their parents' homeland as something more than nostalgic stories and holiday visits.

Nazanin Boroumand, then a college sophomore in New York, describes staying up until dawn translating Persian tweets for her non-Iranian roommates, explaining who Mousavi was, why green mattered, what the Basij represented.

"I realized I knew so little," she admits. "I'd grown up eating my grandmother's *ghormeh sabzi* and half-listening to my parents' stories about the revolution, but I'd never really understood what it meant to lose a country. That summer, I started asking real questions. I started actually listening."

## What Remains

More than a decade later, those weeks in 2009 occupy a peculiar space in diaspora memory—both intensely personal and undeniably historic, private family terror interwoven with global news coverage.

The technology has since evolved. Encrypted apps like Telegram and Signal offer more secure channels than the improvised proxy servers of 2009. But the emotional architecture Iranian-Americans built that summer—the vigilance, the code words, the frame-by-frame scanning of protest footage—established patterns that would resurface during subsequent crises: the 2019 protests, the 2022 Mahsa Amini uprising, each one reactivating old habits of watching, waiting, and reaching across the distance.

"I still flinch when I see a notification from an unknown number," Delshad admits. "Some part of me is still waiting for that call telling me something happened to someone I love, and I can't do anything but listen."

For a diaspora community perpetually suspended between two homes, the summer of 2009 offered a bitter clarity: technology could carry their voices across oceans, but it could not close the distance that mattered most—the one between fear and safety, between waiting and knowing, between a phone call and a hand actually held.
